sections.html:
Columbus is the seat and the only city of Lowndes County, which hugs the Alabama line on Mississippi's eastern side. The count was 58,879 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 57,346, a decline of 2.6 percent. Housing demand is steady rather than booming, tied to manufacturing, Columbus Air Force Base and the Mississippi University for Women.

Two public school systems serve the county, the Columbus Municipal School District and the Lowndes County School District, and the tax bill depends partly on which one covers your address. Each taxing body picks its own levy, and the sum becomes your millage rate. Towns such as Caledonia, Artesia and Crawford, plus rural areas to the west, make up the rest of the market for sellers.

The Tax Office is at 1121 Main Street in Columbus, MS 39701. Call 662-329-5700 to reach the tax collector, or 662-329-3940 for the assessor's mapping line. The county's own site is lowndescountyms.com. Search results for a similarly named county in another state can show a different due date, so stay on that address.

TaskWhere to do it
Pay property tax or car tagsTax Office counter, or the county's online portal at lowndes.ibcpayments.com
Look up a parcel and its tax statusProperty Link real property search, run by Delta Computer Systems
Check a parcel map or boundaryAssessor's mapping line, 662-329-3940, or the appraisal maps from Tri-State Consulting Services
Ask about a payoff on past-due yearsTax Office, 662-329-5700

A parcel lookup is the best first step before you talk to any buyer: the record shows the assessed value, the ratio applied and whether any year is open. The Tax Office page has the current office hours, so look there or call before you drive in.

sections.h2: When Lowndes County property taxes are due
sections.html:
The bill covers the prior year's assessment and must be paid on or before February 1. Should that day be a weekend or legal holiday, Monday becomes the last penalty-free day. Ownership is fixed on January 1, and the statement shows up in the mail around November or December.

  • January 1 to April 1: window to apply for homestead exemption.
  • First Monday in August: usual deadline to appeal with the Board of Supervisors.
  • February 1: payment due.
  • Past February 1: one-half of one percent interest each month.

If you are listing in the fall, ask the buyer's side early who is taking the bill that arrives in November or December. The usual approach is to split the bill by closing date, and the split belongs in writing in the contract or on the settlement statement.

If the value looks wrong, ask the Chancery Clerk to put you on the Board of Supervisors' hearing list. Plan to do it by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

Real property in Mississippi has to be revalued at least once every four years, so your number can move when your parcel comes up. Interior inspections of houses are not required, and the assessor values every structure on a parcel, outbuildings included. If your house was recorded at the wrong size, a refund for earlier years may be possible through the Chancery Clerk.

Before you file, ask the assessor's staff to walk you through the value on the roll. Bring photos, any recent appraisal and recent sales of similar houses.

Homestead exemption covers the house you live in. Take the application to the assessor in the county where the house stands before April 1, and not earlier than January 1. It carries over from year to year, but you should file again if your marital status or ownership changes.

Homeowners 65 or older, and owners who are totally disabled, can be exempt on the first $75,000 of true value if otherwise eligible. Proof of disability may include a VA release form, a Social Security benefit report or letters from two physicians. Falling behind on state income tax filings, for you or a spouse, can cost you eligibility, and so can registering a vehicle in a different county.

An inherited house that no one lives in gets no homestead, so expect the 15 percent ratio on it rather than 10.

Land with unpaid taxes is offered at the county tax sale, and the former owner keeps a two-year right to buy it back. A redeeming owner pays the delinquent taxes, the buyer's money comes back with monthly interest, and if two years pass with no redemption the buyer can get a tax deed from the chancery clerk. The county has run its sale online through GovEase.

State law allows sales on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August, so ask the Tax Office for the date in force. For land already sold to the state, call the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637.

For an owner who is behind, the simplest fix is a sale that closes before the auction date, with the title company paying the taxes out of the proceeds. If the auction has already happened, the redemption amount is the figure to get, and the Chancery Clerk or the Tax Office can supply it. Keep the paperwork from any payment, because a buyer's title company will ask to see it.

A sale here follows the usual Mississippi steps: title search, a prepared deed, payment of taxes and liens at closing, and recording with the chancery clerk.

  1. Pull the parcel on the Property Link search and read the assessed value and tax status.
  2. Get a payoff number from the Tax Office for each year that is past due.
  3. Confirm whether homestead is on file. It is the difference between a 10 percent ratio on a home you occupy and 15 percent on everything else.
  4. For an inherited house, the chancery court handles probate and the clerk files the papers.
  5. Pick an attorney or title company early so the deed and closing are ready.

Owners in Columbus, Caledonia, New Hope and the rural west sometimes sell as-is because of repairs, a move for work or an estate. A cash buyer closes without a bank appraisal or a lender's repair list. Cash Home Buyers reviews every Lowndes County house on its own facts, and we name no price or closing date until we have seen the details.

Bring your deed, a recent tax receipt and any mortgage payoff statement to the first conversation with a title company. Those three papers answer most of the early questions about who owns the house and what is owed.

faqs.q: When are Lowndes County, MS property taxes due?
faqs.a: The deadline is February 1. A Saturday, Sunday or holiday deadline rolls to Monday, and any bill paid after that picks up one-half of one percent a month.

faqs.q: Where is the Lowndes County Tax Office?
faqs.a: It is at 1121 Main Street in Columbus, MS 39701, phone 662-329-5700. An online county portal takes real property tax, personal property tax and car tag payments.

faqs.q: What is the Lowndes County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: Usually the first Monday in August. Contact the Chancery Clerk to get a hearing in front of the Board of Supervisors.

faqs.q: How do I confirm I am on the right county website?
faqs.a: Use lowndescountyms.com, the Mississippi county's site. A similarly named site for a county in another state lists a different due date.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Lowndes County house if taxes are overdue?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays back taxes from your proceeds at closing. A parcel the county has already auctioned stays redeemable for two years from the auction date.
